messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Call Center Agent
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 73

She came to the United States from Bogotá in her early twenties, bringing little more than a sewing machine and a small leather suitcase. Now, at seventy-eight, she has lived more years in this country than she ever did in Colombia. Every morning, she walks the mile and a half to the call center where she works the early shift. She has been a customer service agent for twenty-three years. She knows the route by heart—past the bodega with the torn awning, the bus stop where the teenagers loiter, the metal grate over the subway entrance she stopped using after the explosion.

The explosion happened six years ago, in the summer. She had just exited the train at the station near her apartment. There was a sound she still cannot describe to herself without flinching. Not a bang, not a boom—something thicker and more final, like the world snapping shut. Then the lights went out, and the dust filled her mouth, and she could not breathe. People were running, but she could not move. She stood in the dark, feeling the heat of something burning nearby, and listened to the screaming. When the emergency lights flickered on, she saw the shredded metal, the blood pooled under the turnstiles, the man on the ground whose leg was no longer attached to his body. She stared at him until a paramedic pulled her by the elbow and led her up the stairs into the daylight.

For the first few months afterward, she did not speak about it. She stopped taking the subway entirely, even though it meant walking an extra forty minutes each way. Her daughter, who lives in another state, called every Sunday and asked how she was doing. She always said she was fine. She tried to go back to the way things were—her shifts at the call center, her evening soup, the telenovelas she watched until her eyes grew heavy. But the world had changed. The sound of a car backfiring on her street sent her heart pounding so hard she thought she would collapse. She began to check the locks on her door three times before bed, and then four times, and then five.

At work, she has learned to manage what she calls her *nervios*. When a customer raises his voice on the phone, she feels the dust in her throat again. She grips the edge of her desk, presses her fingernails into her palms, and counts the tiles on the ceiling until the call ends. Her supervisor, a young woman named Jennifer, once commented that she seems “jumpy.” She laughed it off, said it was just her age. She never told anyone what she saw. She is certain that if she did, the images would become real again—crystallized in the telling, impossible to push back into the shadows where she keeps them.

She dreams of the man without a leg. In the dream, he is always standing, walking toward her, leaving a trail of blood on the white tile. She wakes up gasping, her nightgown soaked with sweat, and lies still until the sun rises through the blinds. She avoids the news, especially anything about bombings or shootings, but sometimes a headline catches her eye in the grocery store checkout line and she cannot look away. Her chest tightens. She puts down her basket and leaves.

She has not taken a single day off in the past two years. When her daughter called to invite her for Christmas, she said she had to work. The truth is, she cannot imagine being away from the small, predictable world of her cubicle—the hum of the computer, the script she knows by heart, the rhythm of dial tones and recorded disclaimers. It is the only place where she can pretend, for a few hours at a time, that she is still the person she was before the summer of the explosion. But even here, the memories hover at the edge of her vision, waiting for a moment of silence to rush back in. She does not talk about them. She does not think about them, if she can help it. She simply walks home, checks the locks, and waits for morning.
